By  Giovanni Colantonio
Published Sep 15, 2026, 3:31 PM EDT
Analysis

The stakes are high for PS5's next big exclusive

God of War Laufey now has a lot to prove after Wolverine’s messy launch

Summary

Instaread

A full five years after its announcement, Marvel’s Wolverine is finally out on PlayStation 5. What should be a triumphant moment for Sony, though, has turned out to be an unexpected headache. Uneven reviews, a particularly loud peanut gallery, and close proximity to multiple unpopular business decisions have turned what many assumed would be a surefire bet into a strangely toxic game release.

✕ Remove Ads

It’s certainly not unusual for a publisher to drop a middling game every now and then, but the timing couldn’t be worse for Sony. Aside from managing an optics crisis tied to its decision to end physical disc production in 2028, Wolverine is coming at a time when it's imperative for Sony to find its groove after years of strategic uncertainty. Expect that tension to put even more pressure on its next big first-party game, God of War Laufey.

God of War Laufey - Introducing Faye

Slated to launch on Feb. 16, 2027, God of War Laufey isn’t a very risky game on paper. It’s par for the course for the PS5 era, with Santa Monica Studio looking to deliver the kind of cinematic action-adventure game that PlayStation successfully built its brand around over the past few console generations. In any other year, it would be entering 2027 as a strong Game of the Year contender, considering God of War’s past success with critics and audiences alike.

Instead, God of War Laufey will no doubt have a target painted on its back in the lead up to its launch. There are several reasons for that, some of which have already been foreshadowed by Wolverine. Insomniac’s game had the misfortune of being the first Sony game to release after its physical game announcement. That made it a lightning rod for online anger; any trailer for it or post about it was met with angry commenters using the game as an outlet for anti-PlayStation protest. Wolverine was also another target in gaming’s engagement-driven culture war, and the same fate is all but assured for the first God of War game starring a female character rather than Kratos. (Indeed, this has already begun.) As headache-inducing as those conversations are, though, there’s little data to suggest that either has an impact on sales.

God of War Laufey has already become a culture war disaster

Here we go again...

80

Laufey’s bigger challenge is a more existential one: It needs to prove that audiences still have an appetite for Sony’s brand of big budget games.

One of Wolverine’s problems, according to critics, is that it leans too heavily on design clichés that have become a hallmark of Sony’s award-winning games. There are flashy quick-time events that aren't terribly consequential. There are slow walk-and-talks used to dole out the emotional story. There’s a scent trail that points you towards objectives and collectibles, something that became a point of hyperfocus for players ahead of launch (and which Insomniac Games recently hinted at addressing). If these design tidbits sound familiar, it’s probably because you’ve seen them in other Sony games that put cinematic immersion above all.

✕ Remove Ads

There’s a reason that’s become standard for Sony: It has a long history of paying off. Games like The Last of Us Part 2, God of War (2018), and Marvel’s Spider-Man have all utilized that design philosophy to great effect, turning Sony’s first-party games into both critical darlings and sales behemoths. Wolverine feels like it could be a tipping point for some players, though. For those who are sick of that specific kind of game, it’s easy to point to a less successful example of the formula and use it to argue that the style is dated wholesale.

That puts Laufey in a weird spot. Based on what we’ve seen so far, it looks like it's cut from the same cloth as Wolverine. Its 25-minute gameplay reveal is typical PlayStation blockbuster fare, with cinematic cutscenes weaving in and out of high-octane action. For those who want to make the case that all of Sony’s games follow the same telegraphed patterns, it will be easy to turn it into a soapbox speech about the problems with modern gaming. Santa Monica Studio will have to counter that by delivering an exceptional experience that proves Wolverine is not a synecdoche for the industry at large.

For what it’s worth, I don’t believe it is. As much as I tore into Marvel’s Wolverine in my review, little of my criticism had to do with its adherence to Sony’s formula. The scent trails are fine; the shallow combat that doesn’t really support 15 hours of battling against the same enemy types is a more pressing problem. It’s tempting to conflate those issues in order to build the confirmation-bias narrative that Sony’s style of game is dated, but that feels a bit disingenuous. The simpler explanation may just be that Wolverine simply isn’t as finely designed as some of its peers. It doesn’t need to be more complicated than that, does it?

✕ Remove Ads

But the pressure is on for God of War Laufey regardless. Sony needs a reliable hit to start 2027 if it's going to gain control of a narrative that spun off its axis in 2026. Another perceived miss will leave its style of breadwinning blockbuster vulnerable to scrutiny. Maybe that wouldn’t be such a bad thing; 2024’s award-winning Astro Bot proved that PS5 owners are hungry for a wider variety of single-player games. Sony could stand to get creative and stray away from its big-budget instincts more often. That’s just not the kind of move you want to be making in a do-or-die scenario, and the stakes are higher than they’ve ever been.

    Nah, if the game was undeniable, it'd have been fine. The problem is that the bar is set so high that a "B/B+" game as a Sony first-party exclusive is a huge letdown for the very loud capital-G Gamer crowd that can't regulate their emotions. Plus all the additional (idiotic) right-wing culture war nonsense that capital-G Gamers always bring and the (rightful) anti-Sony sentiment that is a direct result of capitalism doing a capitalism meant there were a lot more people who care to complain at this moment who would have otherwise sat it out.


    There are more character-based design constraints in Wolverine (that you got into a little bit) that make it a less compelling game than there is character fatigue. Because pretty much all of the things that make Wolverine "special" (being good at fighting, being able to take a lot of damage and not go down, being agile and aggressive) are features that literally every video game character in an action/adventure game has had in the last 20 years. Every character can soak damage and kill hundreds of people. Wolverine isn't even known for stealth (which is another thing that every single game character can now do well). What Wolverine has going for him is history and personality. He's a compelling character to write a story about because of his semi-immortality and the way he has experienced the world, but he's not a compelling character to embody. (Unlike Spidey, who is both compelling to tell stories with AND compelling to embody.) Not sure if an ensemble would have been better, but I'm not surprised that a big-budget Wolverine game ended up being "good, not great."

    The first time I saw the gameplay for Wolverine, the exaggerated violence bothered me immediately. Even before Wolverine, I'd noticed that I can scroll through every game store for as long as I want and feel like I'm finding almost nothing but games that glorify violence. It drives me crazy. It's not that I don't want to play games with violence at all. But the ratio of violence-glorifying games has by now gone completely beyond reasonable limits. And if I then take what's left and factor in quality, there isn't much left at all.


    The games industry has taken a path here that let it get away with taking the easy route for far too long. And I think one target group has been neglected in the process. One that also deserves good games: children. Nintendo takes a different approach here, but unfortunately swings to the other extreme. Nintendo's games are often suitable for children, but the sweet spot of roughly 8 to 14 years old somehow isn't covered. Not by Nintendo, and not by Sony or Xbox either. This isn't a platform problem.


    The games industry needs to rediscover itself and make games that are actually fun. Dream up new games and stories instead of constantly churning out yet another sequel in an existing franchise. That takes courage, and the people behind God of War have at least proven, in that one instance, that they have it. Still, what I really want back is games with depth. Ones that don't live off gore alone, but off atmosphere and attention to detail. That's exactly what got lost somewhere along the way, between fans of the medium and dollar signs.
